title: Saudi Astronauts in Space
summary: How Rayyanah Barnawi and Ali AlQarni traveled to the International Space Station in 2023, lived in microgravity, did experiments with students on Earth, and became a milestone for Saudi Arabia.
poll: Sending astronauts to space is a good way to get students interested in science.

versions.title: Up to Space
versions.text:
Look up at the sky. Far up, there is a big lab. It is a space station. It goes round the Earth. It is very fast. It goes round in just an hour and a half.

In May 2023, two Saudis went there. One was Rayyanah Barnawi. She is a scientist. She was the first Saudi woman in space. The other was Ali AlQarni. He flies fast jets.

A big rocket took them up. It left from a place in the USA. Two more astronauts went, too. The four were a crew.

In space, things float. Food can float. A pen can float. You can float, too! So the crew tie things down. They sleep in bags on the wall.

The two did tests on cells. A test like this is an experiment. Kids back home did the same tests in class. Then they could look. Was the test the same in space?

The trip took ten days. Then the crew came back. They fell in the sea. A boat got them.

Their land was so proud of them. Now more kids dream of space.

versions.title: Saudi Astronauts in Space
versions.text:
Look up at the sky on a clear night. Far above you, a large lab is flying around the Earth. It is called the International Space Station. It circles the whole planet in about an hour and a half.

In May 2023, two Saudi astronauts traveled to this station. One was Rayyanah Barnawi. She is a scientist who studies cells in the human body. She became the first Saudi woman to go to space. The other was Ali AlQarni, a fighter pilot in the Saudi air force.

A powerful rocket carried them up. It blasted off from Florida in the United States. Two more astronauts flew with them, so the crew had four people in all.

On the station, everything seems to float. Water forms round drops in the air. Pens drift away if you let them go. People float, too! The crew must strap down their tools and sleep in bags fixed to the wall.

The Saudi astronauts did many science tests. Each test was called an experiment. Some looked at how cells change in space. At the same time, students in Saudi Arabia did the same experiments at school. Then they compared the results from Earth and space.

The trip lasted about ten days. Then the crew rode home and splashed down in the sea. A ship picked them up.

Their journey made the whole country proud. It also showed young people that they can reach for the stars.

The launch took place in Florida in the United States. A strong rocket carried a small spacecraft into the sky. Two other astronauts flew with the Saudis, so the crew had four members.

On the station, the crew lived in microgravity. This means that everything seems to float. Water forms round drops that hang in the air. A pen drifts away if you let it go. So the crew must strap down their tools, and they sleep in bags tied to the wall.

The Saudi astronauts did many experiments. Some looked at how human cells act in space. At the same time, thousands of students in Saudi Arabia did the same kinds of tests in class. Then they compared the results from Earth with the results from space.

The mission lasted about ten days. Then the crew came back and splashed down in the sea near Florida. A ship picked them up.

Their trip made the whole country proud. It also showed young people that study and hard work can help them reach for the stars.

versions.title: Saudi Astronauts in Space
versions.text:
On a clear night, you might notice a bright dot sliding quickly across the sky. It is not a star or a plane. It is the International Space Station, a huge laboratory that circles the Earth about 400 kilometers above the ground. It moves so fast that each orbit, or complete trip around the planet, takes only about ninety minutes.

In May 2023, two Saudi astronauts joined a mission to this station. Rayyanah Barnawi is a scientist who has spent years studying cells in the human body, and she became the first Saudi woman to travel to space. Ali AlQarni is a fighter pilot in the Royal Saudi Air Force who has flown many kinds of jets.

The launch took place at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, in the United States. A tall rocket lifted a small spacecraft into the sky, and about a day later it joined the station. Two other astronauts flew with the Saudis, including an experienced American commander.

On the station, the crew lived in microgravity, which makes everything seem to float. Water forms wobbly balls in the air, and a pen drifts away if nobody holds it. Astronauts strap down their tools, and they sleep in small bags fixed to the walls.

The Saudi astronauts carried out many experiments. Several of them studied how human cells change in space. At the same time, thousands of students in Saudi Arabia performed similar experiments in their classrooms, so they could compare the results from Earth with the results from space. The astronauts also spoke with students by video call.

After about ten days, the crew returned and splashed down in the sea near Florida. Their mission made the country proud and encouraged young people to study science.

The Saudi astronauts carried out many experiments. Several examined how human cells change in microgravity, because this knowledge could help doctors on Earth. Meanwhile, thousands of students in Saudi Arabia performed similar experiments in their classrooms, so they could compare results from Earth with results from space. The astronauts also answered students' questions during a live video call.

After about ten days, the crew returned and splashed down in the sea near Florida. Their mission made the country proud and encouraged young people to dream of careers in science.

versions.title: Saudi Astronauts in Space
versions.text:
On a clear night, an observant person might notice a bright dot gliding steadily across the sky. It is neither a star nor an airplane. It is the International Space Station, an enormous orbiting laboratory that travels about 400 kilometers above the ground. It moves so rapidly that each orbit, or complete journey around the planet, takes only about ninety minutes, which means the crew witnesses roughly sixteen sunrises every day.

In May 2023, two Saudi astronauts joined a mission to this station, and the event became a historic milestone for the Kingdom. The only Saudi to reach space before them was Prince Sultan bin Salman, who flew on an American space shuttle in 1985. Rayyanah Barnawi is a biomedical scientist who spent years doing research on cells in the human body, including cells connected to breast cancer, and she became the first Saudi woman to travel to space. Ali AlQarni is a fighter pilot in the Royal Saudi Air Force with extensive experience operating jets.

The launch took place on May 21 at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, in the United States. A powerful rocket lifted a small capsule into orbit, and the following day the capsule connected to the station. Two other astronauts traveled with the Saudis, including an experienced American commander who had already spent hundreds of days in space during earlier missions.

On the station, the crew lived in microgravity, a condition that makes everything appear to float. Drops of water become trembling spheres, and a pen drifts away unless somebody holds it. Astronauts secure their equipment with straps, exercise every day so their muscles and bones remain strong, and sleep in small bags fastened to the walls.

The Saudi astronauts conducted many experiments. Several examined how human cells change in microgravity, because this information could eventually help doctors treat illnesses on Earth. Meanwhile, thousands of students throughout Saudi Arabia performed similar experiments in their classrooms, allowing them to compare results from Earth with results from space. The astronauts also answered students' questions during a live video call from orbit.

After about ten days, the crew returned to Earth, and the capsule made a gentle splashdown in the sea near Florida. The mission made the nation proud, and many people hope it will inspire young Saudis to consider careers in science and engineering.

It is neither a star nor an airplane but the International Space Station, an enormous laboratory that orbits about 400 kilometers above the planet's surface. Because the station travels at tremendous speed, it completes each orbit in about ninety minutes, so its crew sees roughly sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets every day.

In May 2023, two Saudi astronauts traveled to this station, and their journey became a historic milestone for the Kingdom, which had not sent a citizen into space since Prince Sultan bin Salman flew on an American space shuttle in 1985. Rayyanah Barnawi is a biomedical scientist who spent years doing research on human cells, including cells connected to breast cancer, and she became the first Saudi woman to reach space. Ali AlQarni is a skilled fighter pilot in the Royal Saudi Air Force who brought long experience flying high-performance jets.

The launch took place on May 21 at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, in the United States, where a powerful rocket lifted a small capsule into orbit. The next day, the capsule connected to the station. Two other astronauts traveled with the Saudis, including an experienced American commander who had already spent hundreds of days in space during earlier missions.

Aboard the station, the crew lived in microgravity, a condition that makes objects seem to float. Drops of water become trembling spheres, and a pen drifts away unless somebody holds it. For this reason, astronauts secure their equipment with straps, exercise daily so their muscles and bones stay strong, and sleep in small bags fastened to the walls.

The Saudi astronauts carried out many experiments, and several of them examined how human cells behave in microgravity, because this knowledge could one day help doctors treat diseases on Earth. Meanwhile, thousands of students across Saudi Arabia performed similar experiments in their classrooms, so they could compare results gathered on the ground with results gathered in orbit. The astronauts also answered students' questions during a live video call.

After about ten days, the crew returned to Earth, and the capsule made a gentle splashdown in the sea near Florida. Many people hope the mission will inspire a new generation of Saudi scientists, engineers, and explorers.

versions.title: Saudi Astronauts in Space
versions.text:
On a clear night, an attentive observer might notice a brilliant dot gliding steadily across the darkness, which is neither a star nor an airplane but the International Space Station, an enormous laboratory orbiting roughly 400 kilometers above the planet's surface. Because the station travels at tremendous velocity, it completes each orbit in approximately ninety minutes, so its residents experience about sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets every day.

In May 2023, two Saudi astronauts traveled to this orbiting laboratory, and their journey represented a historic milestone for the Kingdom, whose only earlier astronaut, Prince Sultan bin Salman, had flown aboard an American space shuttle in 1985. Rayyanah Barnawi is a biomedical scientist who devoted years to research on human cells, particularly cells associated with breast cancer, and she became the first Saudi woman to reach space. Ali AlQarni is an accomplished fighter pilot in the Royal Saudi Air Force who brought long experience flying fast, high-performance jets.

The launch occurred on May 21 at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, in the United States, where a powerful rocket propelled a compact capsule into orbit, and the following day the capsule docked with the station. Two additional astronauts accompanied the Saudis, including an experienced American commander who had previously accumulated hundreds of days in space during earlier expeditions.

Aboard the station, the crew lived in microgravity, a condition in which objects appear to float effortlessly. Droplets of water become trembling spheres, and an unattended pen gradually drifts away. Consequently, astronauts secure their equipment with straps, exercise every day so that their muscles and bones remain healthy, and sleep in small bags fastened to the walls.

The Saudi astronauts conducted numerous experiments, several of which investigated how human cells behave in microgravity, because such knowledge could one day help doctors treat diseases on Earth. At the same time, thousands of students throughout Saudi Arabia performed similar experiments in their classrooms, which allowed them to compare observations gathered on the ground with results collected in orbit. The astronauts also answered students' questions during a live video conversation.

After approximately ten days, the crew returned to Earth, and the capsule completed a gentle splashdown in the sea near Florida. Many people hope that this remarkable mission will inspire a new generation of Saudi scientists, engineers, and explorers. Indeed, the Saudi Space Agency has described the expedition as only the beginning of a longer program, in which the Kingdom intends to train additional astronauts and take a larger part in international space exploration.

An important event that marks progress
A small mistake in a plan
questions.why: A milestone is an important event that shows progress; this mission was a big step for Saudi Arabia in space.

wrong.A: That is a literal stone, not the meaning used here.
wrong.B: A milestone is an achievement, not a delay.
wrong.D: A milestone is a success, not a mistake.

questions.stem: Why does the crew of the station see about sixteen sunrises every day?
options: The Sun moves faster when seen from space.
The station circles Earth about every ninety minutes.
The station has bright lamps that look like the Sun.
Astronauts sleep for only a few minutes at a time.
questions.why: Each orbit takes about ninety minutes, and in each orbit the crew passes from night into day once, which adds up to about sixteen sunrises.

wrong.A: The article explains the sunrises by the station's speed, not by the Sun moving.
wrong.D: Sleep has nothing to do with how many sunrises there are.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why students across Saudi Arabia joined the experiments?
options: It linked the mission to learning in schools across the country.
The astronauts did not have time to finish their own work.
The students' results were sent to the commander to grade.
The schools needed to test their new equipment.
questions.why: Having students compare their results with results from orbit connected the mission to classrooms, which fits the hope that it would inspire young Saudis.

wrong.B: The astronauts did their own experiments; students did similar ones on the ground.
wrong.C: Nothing suggests the commander graded anything.
wrong.D: Testing school equipment is not the purpose given.

questions.stem: What does the last paragraph suggest about the long-term goal of the mission?
options: To prove that the capsule could land on dry ground
To announce that Saudi Arabia's space program is now finished
To encourage young Saudis to choose careers in science and exploration
To show that one mission is enough
questions.why: The last paragraph hopes the mission will inspire a new generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers.

wrong.A: The capsule landed in the sea, not on ground.
wrong.B: The article suggests a beginning, not an end.
wrong.D: The hope for a new generation shows that more is expected.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe floating water drops and drifting pens?
options: To warn readers not to drink water in space
To prove that pens do not work in space
To compare the station with an airplane
To help readers imagine what microgravity is like
questions.why: Concrete pictures of floating drops and drifting pens make the idea of microgravity easy to imagine.

wrong.A: The author does not warn against drinking water.
wrong.B: The pens drift away; the article does not say they stop working.
wrong.C: The airplane is only mentioned when describing the light in the sky, not in this part.

HIGH.prompt: The author says many people hope this mission will inspire a new generation. Explain how the mission could inspire students, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
HIGH.modelAnswer: This mission could inspire students because it shows what hard work and study can achieve, since Rayyanah Barnawi became the first Saudi woman in space as a scientist who studies human cells. The article also explains that thousands of students in Saudi Arabia ran their own experiments in their classrooms while the astronauts conducted similar research aboard the International Space Station, giving students a direct connection to a historic research milestone and showing that they too could reach for the stars.
